rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.9 describe a two-year (2017-2018) split-plot field experiment in a commercial Cabernet Sauvignon vineyard near Benton City, WA, with own measurements. Q2: Section 3.5 and Table 3 report that irrigation method had significant effects on yield in both years, with about 9% (2017) and 12% (2018) higher yield under DRZ than SD across all irrigation rates (SD 9.2/9.3 vs DRZ 10.0/10.4 t/ha). Q4: Section 3.3 and Fig. 3 report midday stem water potential measured by pressure chamber, 10-14% higher under DRZ than SD after veraison in both years; Discussion links lower water stress under DRZ to more resources for aboveground growth and higher yield. Q8: Discussion and Conclusions state the study is an initial step, results are for loamy sand in a semi-arid climate, the proposed mechanisms (reduced evaporation, deep roots) need testing in future studies, and a long-term (e.g. 10-year) study is needed to identify desirable conditions and evaluate benefits.
rows.notes: Yield was measured by one method (hand harvest and weighing) only. One site, one crop, one soil; plot-scale (15-vine plots) only. Soil-texture conditions in the Discussion are drawn from other studies, not the authors' own findings; the root-number interaction with irrigation rate is a variation, not a stated requirement. Table 3 gives yield means with Tukey letters only, no SD/SE/CI; the 9-12% figure is a range across two years, not a dispersion measure. Q4 'yes' rests on stem water potential as the measured intermediate; soil evaporation and soil water in treatment plots were not measured.

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.9 describe the authors' own two-year field experiment in a commercial vineyard with three irrigation rates and two methods. Q2: Table 3 and Section 3.5-3.6 report DRZ increased yield about 9% and 12% and WUEc 9-11% versus surface drip in 2017 and 2018; Section 4 notes the different weather between years did not change the treatment effects on yield and WUEc. Q4: Section 3.3/Fig. 3 report midday stem water potential 10-14% higher under DRZ after veraison in both years, interpreted in Section 4 as lower water stress leaving more carbon and nitrogen for production. Q8: Section 4 and Conclusions describe the study as an initial step, limited to loamy sand in a semi-arid climate, with mechanisms untested and a long-term study needed to define optimum conditions.
rows.notes: The review passage says DRZ was contrasted with 'SDI', but the study compares DRZ with surface drip (SD); DRZ itself is the subsurface variant. The technology is still a drip system, so no mismatch flagged. Yield and WUEc rest on one measurement method; single site and crop; plot scale; no dispersion statistics for yield or WUEc in Table 3 (means with Tukey letters only).

rows.evidence: Q1: Own two-year field experiment (Sections 2.1-2.9). Q2: Section 3.6 and Table 3 report WUEc (yield per unit of irrigation plus rainfall from bud break to harvest) significantly affected by irrigation method, with DRZ improving WUEc by 9-11% over SD (35.1 vs 38.3 and 39.3 vs 43.8 kg/ha/mm); Section 4 notes variable weather between years did not change this effect. Q4: Section 3.3/Fig. 3 report higher midday stem water potential under DRZ after veraison, which the Discussion uses to explain more available water and higher WUEc. Q8: Conclusions state that reduced evaporation and deep rooting as causes still need testing, that results apply to loamy sand in a semi-arid climate, and that desirable conditions for DRZ require a long-term study.
rows.notes: WUEc here is yield per unit applied water with identical water applied across methods, so the WUE gain is the yield gain; soil evaporation (the authors' proposed water-saving mechanism) was not measured, only asserted. Q4 is based on measured plant water status as intermediate. Single method, single site/crop, plot scale; Table 3 reports means with Tukey letters only, no dispersion.

rows.evidence: Q1: Own two-year field experiment (Sections 2.1-2.9). Q2: Section 3.3, Table 1 and Fig. 3 report that grapevines under DRZ had significantly 10-14% higher midday stem water potential than under SD after veraison in both years, during the period with extremely limited rainfall and increasing temperature (Supplemental Table 1, Section 4), i.e. reduced water stress under seasonal drought; Table 4 reports irrigation rate changed berry weight, diameter and number. Q8: Conclusions state that deep root development and reduced evaporation 'could be' the reasons for lower water stress and need to be tested in future studies; the study is described as an initial step with a long-term study required.
rows.notes: The study's own evidence supports lower water stress under DRZ; however 'deep rooting' was not measured (minirhizotron only to 60 cm) and is inferred from fewer roots in the 0-60 cm profile, so the mechanism named in the passage is speculative, hence Q4 'no'. Stem water potential was the sole method for water status. Single site/crop, plot scale. Fig. 3 reports Tukey letters only (no error bars mentioned); SE bars appear only for root counts (Figs 4, 6, 7), not for the water-stress result.

notes: Full text appears complete. The study compares direct root-zone irrigation (a subsurface drip variant delivering water via vertical PVC tubes at 60 cm) with surface drip irrigation in one commercial vineyard on loamy sand in semi-arid Washington over 2017-2018, with three irrigation rates. Some review passages mislabel the comparator as SDI.
